strengths: The paper addresses a highly practical and challenging problem in image-to-video (I2V) generation: ensuring precise interaction between an actor and a specific target object.
The proposed method is technically sound, cleanly combining mask-channel concatenation, a special [TGT] token, and a targeted cross-attention loss.

The paper offers an insightful analysis of multi-modal diffusion transformer (MM-DiT) architectures, explaining why supervising video-to-text (V2T) attention is superior to text-to-video (T2V) attention, and why standard attention modulation fails.

Both qualitative and quantitative evaluations are thorough, demonstrating a substantial boost in target-interaction accuracy (measured via contact score and user studies) without compromising overall video quality.
The demonstrated downstream applications—depth-aware human insertion for video creation and physics-based imitation learning—are creative and highly convincing.
weaknesses: The dataset size used for fine-tuning (1,290 clips) and evaluation (50 images) is relatively small. A larger-scale evaluation would further validate the robustness of the approach.

The approach assumes a static camera setting (inherent to the curated dataset), which limits its applicability to dynamic camera movements where a static first-frame mask might not align well over time.

The paper lacks comparisons with some of the more recent layout-controlled or trajectory-guided video generation baselines, comparing instead with simpler drag-based or attention-modulation baselines.
The inference speed is quite slow (~4 minutes per video on an A100), which limits real-time or interactive usage, although this is largely a constraint of the underlying CogVideoX-5B model.

strengths: The paper addresses a highly practical and challenging problem in controllable image-to-video generation: ensuring that the generated character interacts precisely with a specified target object in the scene without hallucinating or ignoring it.

The technical design is elegant and lightweight. Instead of requiring dense temporal controls (like optical flow or trajectories), it only requires a single segmentation mask of the target in the first frame and a text prompt.

The analysis of the selective cross-attention loss is insightful. The comparison between Video-to-Text (V2T) and Text-to-Video (T2V) attention regions, along with identifying semantically rich transformer blocks, provides valuable technical insights for modern Multi-Modal Diffusion Transformer (MM-DiT) architectures.

The quantitative and qualitative evaluations are thorough, demonstrating significant improvements in target interaction accuracy (via Contact Score and user preference studies) without compromising overall video generation quality.

The downstream application demonstrations, particularly zero-shot 3D HOI motion synthesis in physical simulation (Isaac Gym), highlight the model's strong potential for high-level action planning and robotics.
weaknesses: The fine-tuning dataset is relatively small, consisting of only 1,290 clips. While the model shows some zero-shot generalization, the narrow scope of the training datasets (BEHAVE and Ego-Exo4D) might limit its performance on highly diverse, open-domain interaction scenarios.

Since the target-aware guidance (the segmentation mask) is only applied to the first frame, the model might struggle to maintain object tracking or appearance consistency in later frames during complex or fast-paced physical interactions.

The pipeline for the video content creation and motion synthesis applications is quite complex and heavily relies on multiple external tools (such as SAM, metric depth estimators, and 3D human pose estimators), which can accumulate errors.

strengths: The paper addresses a highly practical and challenging task: achieving precise control over human-object interactions (HOI) in image-to-video generation without requiring dense, frame-by-frame structural guidance.

The proposed method is elegant and simple. Introducing a specialized `[TGT]` token combined with a cross-attention loss that aligns with the target mask effectively guides the video diffusion model to focus on the desired interaction area.

The paper provides an insightful analysis of the attention mechanisms in Multi-Modal Diffusion Transformers (MM-DiTs). Identifying that Video-to-Text (V2T) cross-attention is the key region to supervise for spatial alignment is a useful technical contribution.

The evaluation is thorough. The authors introduce a contact-based metric (using an off-the-shelf hand-object contact detector) alongside standard VBench metrics and detailed user studies to demonstrate a substantial improvement in target accuracy.

The downstream applications are highly compelling, especially the zero-shot 3D HOI motion synthesis, which showcases how the 2D video generation model can serve as a trajectory/action planner to guide physics-based imitation learning in simulators.
weaknesses: The curated training dataset is relatively small, consisting of only 1,290 clips from BEHAVE and Ego-Exo4D. This limited scale could restrict the model's capability to generalize to open-world scenarios or complex multi-step actions.
Due to the static-camera nature of the fine-tuning datasets, the generated videos are constrained to fixed camera trajectories, which limits the flexibility of the generated content.

The mathematical notation in Section 4.2 (Equation 2) is slightly confusing. Using $z_t^0$ to represent the latent noise of the first frame at timestep $t$ mixes the temporal index of the video frames with the diffusion denoising timestep $t$ in a non-standard way. A clearer mathematical formulation would improve readability.

The downstream application pipelines are heavily dependent on a long chain of external models (e.g., metric depth estimators, 3D human mesh reconstructors, physics imitation learning modules), making the overall system complexity high.

strengths: Introduces an important and highly practical task (Target-Aware Video Generation) that bridges the gap between high-level text instructions and spatially grounded interactions, which is of great value to motion planning and robotics.

Proposes a clean and effective technical framework that extends the MM-DiT architecture with an additional mask channel, and aligns the cross-attention map of a special [TGT] token with the mask via a selective cross-attention loss.

Provides a thorough analysis and justification of the selective loss design, explaining why applying the loss to specific transformer blocks and the video-to-text (V2T) attention region yields the best performance on MM-DiTs.

Demonstrates robust quantitative and qualitative performance, outperforming representative baselines (such as attention modulation and drag-based methods) by a large margin on contact-based and user preference metrics while maintaining generation quality.
Conducts comprehensive robustness evaluations showing the model's tolerance to mask quality, mask shapes, noisy training captions, and perturbed inference prompts.

Presents exciting and concrete downstream applications, particularly zero-shot 3D human-object interaction (HOI) motion synthesis combined with physics-based imitation learning in Isaac Gym, bridging the gap between video generation and robotics control.
weaknesses: There is a minor contradiction in the text regarding the selective transformer blocks: Page 5 states that the cross-attention loss is applied to uniformly sampled blocks (every 5th) within the 5-23 range, whereas Appendix A.1 states it is applied to every third transformer block within that range.

The curated training dataset is relatively small (1,290 clips). While the strong prior of the base model (CogVideoX) allows it to generalize well, the scale of target-aware training remains somewhat limited.

As discussed in the limitations, the method is designed for a fixed single target throughout the video and cannot easily handle dynamic target switching or scaling up to many simultaneous targets without architectural changes.

strengths: Highly relevant and practical task: Explicitly specifying an interaction target via a simple mask solves a major limitation of standard image-to-video models, such as target hallucination or interacting with the wrong target.

Well-motivated technical design: Proposing a specific [TGT] token and optimizing its alignment with the mask using Video-to-Text (V2T) attention regions is elegant and matches the unified text-video attention formulation of MM-DiTs.

Extremely thorough evaluation: The use of contact-based metrics (Contact Score, temporal variants, and Interaction Score), standard VBench video quality metrics, and two types of user studies provides strong, multi-dimensional proof of the method's effectiveness.

Comprehensive ablation studies: The paper extensively validates key design choices, such as which transformer blocks to supervise, which attention regions to apply the loss to, the loss weight, and the robustness of the model to mask quality, mask shape, and caption noise.

Inspiring downstream applications: Showing that the generated 2D videos can be used to extract physically plausible 3D HOI motions inside Isaac Gym highlights the potential of video diffusion models as motion planners for robotics.
weaknesses: Scalability to multiple targets: The current architecture concatenates target masks as additional channels and uses a single [TGT] token, which makes it hard to scale to scenes with many different target interactions.

Lack of temporal target switching: The target mask is only specified for the first frame. For highly dynamic objects or very long videos, the model is unable to handle sequential interactions with different targets over time within a single video.
Dependence on the base model: The generation quality and motion range are bounded by the underlying CogVideoX-5B model, which sometimes generates typical synthesis artifacts.

strengths: Highly practical and well-motivated task formulation: target-aware video generation allows directing an actor's interaction with a specific object in the scene, which is extremely useful for robotic motion planning and video content creation.

Technically sound and elegant methodology: the introduction of the special [TGT] token coupled with a selective cross-attention loss in MM-DiT architectures is intuitive and requires minimal parameter overhead (using LoRA and single-channel projection layer extension).

Detailed analysis of attention mechanisms: the paper provides a principled exploration of attention regions, demonstrating why supervising Video-to-Text (V2T) attention is more effective than Text-to-Video (T2V) attention.

Extensive quantitative and qualitative evaluation: the authors evaluate their method using objective contact-detection scores, user studies, and VBench metrics, demonstrating clear improvements over strong baselines without degrading overall video generation quality.

Outstanding robustness evaluations: the ablation studies show that the model is robust to mask quality, mask shape (e.g., working with simple bounding circles instead of precise segmentation), and caption noise.

Impressive downstream applications: the integration with physics-based simulators (Isaac Gym) for zero-shot 3D HOI synthesis and long-term video generation showcases the practical utility of the proposed world-model approach.
weaknesses: Relatively small dataset scale: the curated training dataset contains 1290 clips. While sufficient for LoRA training, evaluation on a larger-scale, more diverse training set would strengthen the generalizability claims.

Inference computational cost: the inference time of ~250 seconds per video on an A100 GPU is quite high, which may limit real-time interactive applications (though this is largely inherited from the CogVideoX-5B base model).

Scalability to multiple targets: as noted in the limitations, the architecture relies on concatenating target masks as extra channels, which does not easily scale to an arbitrary number of targets or dynamic target-switching over time.

Compatibility with traditional U-Net architectures: since the methodology is tailored to modern MM-DiT architectures, the paper would benefit from a discussion or brief experiment on how this attention alignment loss can be adapted to older U-Net-based video diffusion models.
